Barbara Lee has served in Congress for over 25 years. Lee first got involved in politics when she met Shirley Chisholm and worked on Chisholm's presidential campaign in 1972. Chisholm made history as the first black woman in Congress and as the first black woman to seek a presidential nomination from a major political party. Now, with Kamala Harris as our first Black and South Asian woman on the ballot for president, Lee reflects on what Chisholm might think of where we are today and shares her own thoughts on this current political moment. As the first Black woman elected to the State Senate from Northern California and the highest-ranking Black woman appointed to Democratic leadership, Lee has been a trailblazer who has always been a strong advocate for increasing Black women's representation in politics. She is also known for being an outspoken proponent of peace, advancing legislation to address HIV and AIDS and end poverty. Lee coined the phrase War on Women when Republican lawmakers were pushing to strip critical funding for women's health care services. Earlier this year, Lee stepped up to run for the Senate seat vacated after Senator Dianne Feinstein's passing. Although Lee was defeated in the Senate primary and will leave Congress in January, she insists she's, quote, not retiring and will keep working from the outside to, quote, get a lot done. In this insightful interview, the Congresswoman and I discuss what it would mean if Harris is elected as our first woman and women of color president, what's at stake in this coming election and what her call to action is. Why having black women's perspectives and leadership is so important? What we can do to get more women in diversity into politics? What's next for her and more? It is so wonderful to speak to you again. You were always one of my favorite people to talk to. And of course, reflecting back to when I interviewed you all those years ago for my book, What Will It Take to Make a Woman President? A momentous time for us to be talking again. So just to sort of even start there, we are in a historic moment where the U.S. could potentially elect Kamala Harris as our first black and South Asian woman president. What would it mean to young boys and girls in this country and to women's leadership generally to finally break the glass ceiling and elect a woman president who is also a woman of color? If you've seen the picture of all the men, the white guys who've been president, except for President Obama, and you don't see a woman, you don't see a woman of color, you don't see a black woman, this is part of our democracy that has still not been fulfilled. You know, and I think with this race now, what it means is this is another step toward making a more perfect union and living up to our creative liberty and justice for all. The perspective of a black woman is a perspective that because of our experiences, that no other women have had, really. And women, though, when you look at black maternal mortality rates, okay, when you look at issues around criminal justice reform, when you look at issues around specific diseases that people of color are disproportionately represented in. I do a lot, for example, on HIV and AIDS, on lupus, on sickle cell anemia. It's that experience and that understanding of people who have been marginalized and shut out that black women bring to the table, or women of color, or a woman. And so the uniqueness of a perspective helps not only strengthen women, women of color or black women, it helps strengthen the country because black women come with the integrity, the respect, the experience of being caregivers, of being leaders in our community who always educated our young people who have been there for everyone and have been relegated to being behind the scenes, doing the work. Of course, we do the work because we're committed to it. But we have that experience, and we have that knowledge, and we're smart, and we're strong. And when Dr. Maya Angelou, she always says, you know, I am the hopes and the dreams of the slaves, and still I rise. And so I think this country and the world benefits from having a woman like Kamala Harris because of the challenges she's been through, of the experiences, for instance, with her mother as a caregiver. Her mother would cancer. All of this comes to help others and help strengthen this country and help close a lot of the gaps and disrupt many of the barriers and really move forward to help everyone benefit from the American dream, which so many don't at this point.
